Poti Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Poti, Georgia

Not demolished. Poti, a Black Sea port city with roots as a Greek colony dating to the 7th-6th century BCE, drew Jewish traders from Lechkhumi from the early 19th century, with more arriving from Tskhinvali, Sujuna, Bandza, Kutaisi, and Senaki as the port developed. By the early 20th century, the Jewish population reached 850-900 families (541 of them Georgian Jewish, the rest Ashkenazi migrants who arrived after Georgia joined the Russian Empire). A 1902 brick synagogue anchored the community; rabbis included Ashkenazi Moshe Levin, followed by Benzon Levin and later Michael Elashvili (who arrived from Sujuna in 1918). Poti's Jewish population declined sharply under Soviet rule, though it still numbered 1,170 in 1970. Khaim Mikhelashvili and his sons were prominent in the 1970s aliyah rights movement, part of a well-known letter signed by 18 Georgian Jewish families petitioning to emigrate. By the 1980s, only about 50 of 600 Georgian Jewish families remained in Poti; after a second wave of emigration in the 1990s, the synagogue closed. This cemetery holds tombstones from 1906 to 2017.
